# SignalTree

This reference describes the 15.4.3 package version, with explicitly marked
15.3.1 comparisons. Consult the [npm package page](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@signal-tree/kernel?activeTab=versions)
for published versions.

SignalTree keeps nested state, entity identity, transactions, undo, external
updates and reactive publication consistent across frameworks. The v15 construction model is
`signalTree(initialState, { derived, enhancers })`; state is read through
`tree.$`.

## What SignalTree is — and is not

```text
IS:     framework-independent consequential application state, stable subject
      identity, authored versus external authority, coherent operation
      boundaries, causal/restoration semantics, and link-based relationships

IS NOT: primarily an undo library, event log, query library, sync engine, or
      persistence framework
```

Undo/redo, event replay, query composition, live synchronization, and
persistence are all things applications correctly BUILD on top of SignalTree's
causal model — see "Composition patterns" below — but none of them is what
SignalTree is FOR. Describe SignalTree by its primary job (consequential state
with a causal model an application can trust), not by one thing that model
happens to make easy.

The Angular facade supports Angular 20, 21, or 22.

v15 ships five packages under the hyphenated `@signal-tree/*` scope. The
no-hyphen `@signaltree/*` scope is the separate v14 line: still maintained for
bug and security fixes (check the [registry](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@signaltree/core) for the current patch), frozen on features, and not an
alias for anything under `@signal-tree/*`. Generate `@signal-tree/*` names for
new v15 code. The canonical package set is `scripts/release-plan.mjs`:

- `@signal-tree/kernel` — framework-neutral tree, `entityMap()`, causal turns,
  links, and the `restoration()` / `transactions()` / `batching()` / `devTools()`
  enhancers. Also `@signal-tree/kernel/adapter`, the realization SDK.
- `@signal-tree/angular` — the complete Angular application facade. **Angular
  code imports `signalTree` and all other SignalTree APIs from here**. Terminal
  state leaves are native `WritableSignal<T>` values and derived leaves are
  native `Signal<T>` values. Adds `defineStore()` and `toWritableSignal()` for
  adapting callable object branches or designating form ingress.
- `@signal-tree/react` — the complete React application facade. **React code
  imports `signalTree`, markers, enhancers, and `useSignalTree(owner, selector)`
  from here**; React observes the canonical kernel tree without copying it.
- `@signal-tree/vue` — the complete Vue application facade. **Vue code imports
  `signalTree` and all other SignalTree APIs from here**. Terminal state leaves
  are native `Ref<T>` values and derived leaves are `ComputedRef<T>` values.
- `@signal-tree/solid` — the complete Solid application facade. Read terminal
  leaves with `leaf()` and write with `leaf.set(value)`.

Use `@signal-tree/kernel` directly only for framework-neutral TypeScript,
including reusable domain libraries. Framework facades forward the neutral
kernel surface by canonical identity; they do not duplicate semantic authority.

## Accessor grammar and terminal values

The neutral kernel exposes callable locations:

```typescript
import { signalTree } from '@signal-tree/kernel';
const location = signalTree({ count: 0 }).$.count;
location();                       // read
location(5);                      // replace the complete value
location((current) => current + 1); // derive the next complete value
```

The root (`tree.$`) and object branches keep this callable whole-value grammar
in every facade. Terminal values use the framework's native carrier:

```typescript
import { signalTree } from '@signal-tree/angular';
const angularTree = signalTree({ count: 0 });
angularTree.$.count();
angularTree.$.count.set(5);
angularTree.$.count.update((count) => count + 1);
```

```typescript
import { signalTree } from '@signal-tree/solid';
const solidTree = signalTree({ count: 0 });
solidTree.$.count();
solidTree.$.count.set(5);
```

```typescript
import { signalTree } from '@signal-tree/vue';
const vueTree = signalTree({ count: 0 });
vueTree.$.count.value;
vueTree.$.count.value = 5;
```

React has no persistent signal primitive, so `@signal-tree/react` keeps neutral
locations and observes selected state through `useSignalTree(owner, selector)`.
EntityMap query and field leaves follow the same carrier rule; EntityMap command
methods such as `setAll()` and `updateOne()` do not change.

Replace atomic values through their location. In-place mutation of a returned
object, array, Map or Set is not a recorded write; restoration does not provide
deep-copy isolation for mutable payloads.

Plain objects normally become traversable branches. `leaf(value)` explicitly
ends topology so an object remains one atomic location. Declare function-valued
fields with `leaf(fn)`. At a callable write boundary, use `leaf(fn)` to distinguish
a stored function from an updater. Native Angular `.set(fn)` assigns the function
directly, as shown below:

```typescript
import { signalTree, leaf } from '@signal-tree/angular';
const angularTree = signalTree({
  range: leaf({ start: 0, end: 10 }),
  callback: leaf((value: number) => console.log(value)),
});

angularTree.$.range.set({ start: 5, end: 15 });
angularTree.$.callback.set((value) => console.log(value));
```

The wrapper is consumed at construction or invocation and never enters state,
snapshots, persistence, restoration, links, or causal payloads.

There is no v15 forms, persistence, validation, events, or realtime package;
those are application-owned. `.with()`, positional `derived`, and the
`stored`/`asyncSource`/`asyncQuery`/`form`/`status` markers were all removed.

## Migration Rule

Never design SignalTree around a legacy application's intermediate state.

1. Determine the canonical greenfield v15 architecture.
2. Implement and validate that architecture independently.
3. Migrate applications toward that target.
4. Prefer deleting obsolete concepts over adapting them.
5. Never add compatibility APIs merely to reduce migration work.
6. A migration may falsify the target architecture, but legacy usage does not
   define it.

Do not create intermediate APIs intended to be removed later. Do not add
compatibility layers because a migration is large. Do not preserve old
ownership because moving it is inconvenient. Do not design framework adapters
from legacy application idioms. Do not optimize for minimal migration diff.
Optimize for the architecture applications should use five years from now.

`@signal-tree/kernel/adapter` is the SDK for realization ownership, not a
compatibility layer. New exports must be framework-neutral semantic facts owned
by the kernel and required by correct realizations.

## Framework Realization Rule

Framework packages may realize SignalTree truth for their runtime. They must
not create another state authority.

Never use process-global mutable framework installation merely to make a legacy
integration work if construction-bound ownership can express the long-term
architecture. A migration cannot determine realization ownership.

## Framework Ownership Ratchet

`@signal-tree/kernel` owns framework-independent SignalTree semantics.
`@signal-tree/kernel/adapter` owns only neutral ports for semantic questions
the kernel owns. Framework packages own their implementations, lifecycle,
diagnostics, schedulers, rendering behavior, primitive identity rules, and
quirks. Neutral naming does not establish neutral ownership.

Every new realization contract must state its SignalTree semantic job, provide
a neutral implementation, be implementable by a tiny framework-free fake, and
name the kernel authority deciding when and why it runs. Reject contracts that
exist only for one framework. If Angular, React, and Vue disappeared, the
contract must remain meaningful to SignalTree or another reactive runtime.

## Composition patterns

Several capabilities that look like missing features are compositions of
primitives that already ship — see `docs/guides/composition-recipes.md` for
the full recipes with executable-spec citations. Do not propose a new marker
or kernel API for any of these before reading it:

- a standard enhancer policy, a reusable entity-CRUD Ops base, a selection
  read-model
- optimistic writes with server reconciliation (`transactions()`'s
  pending/confirm/rollback lifecycle)
- staged/draft editing (an application-owned draft, one authored commit — no
  `beginStage()` session API)
- one-shot loading (`external()`, no `link()` needed for a single fetch) versus
  a persistent relationship with an external authority (`link()`'s three
  composable directions: PULL/PUSH-IN/PUSH-OUT)
- accepted external truth is distinct from authored application work, so an
  external write is not automatically a retained causal-history turn
- a human-readable explanation projected from the causal record (the
  explanation is a PROJECTION of causal truth — the kernel does not store
  prose, actor names, or timestamps merely to make one convenient)

`docs/guides/persistence-guide.md` is the `link()`-as-storage specialization
of the same model.

## Transaction failure guidance

The failure behavior in this section describes published SignalTree 15.3.1.
The release-tag link below is fixed to 15.3.1 to preserve that historical
comparison; it is not a list of defects in 15.4.0. Check versioned changes against
the installed version; source changes do not update an existing tarball.

Read [Transaction failures and limitations in 15.3.1](https://github.com/JBorgia/signal-tree/blob/v15.3.1/docs/guides/transaction-failures-v15.md)
before generating optimistic writes or persistence. Explicit `pending.rollback()`
refusal leaves state unchanged and the handle pending, but releases consequences
in existing v15. In 15.3.1, automatic refusal before a
handle returns records surviving writes as committed, retains eligible undo
history, releases consequences, and still throws. Successful automatic rollback
reverses recorded writes. Error does not guarantee undo: never blindly retry the
whole operation or use `undo()`/`jumpTo()` for request reconciliation. Since
15.4.2, a pending-created or pending-rekeyed row removed by settled later work
no longer blocks rollback, and since 15.4.4 neither does a field write to an
existing row that settled later work removed; a pending-created row confirmed
work edited and kept still refuses, so removal is not a general recovery
strategy. Since 15.4.4 a pending removal or rename whose key later work gave to
another row refuses as a dependency while that row stands or undo history can
restore it; an order change refuses as a dependency while later work on the
collection stands; and rolling back while a newer pending transaction omitted or
re-added a plain branch enclosing an older write refuses with
`later-pending-dependency`. Settle the newer transaction first. Since 15.4.4,
after a rejection no `undo()`, `redo()` or `jumpTo()` reinstates a value or row
that only the rejected transaction wrote. Recoverable pending refusal is a v16
target, not v15 API.

15.3.1 containment covers deferred write subscribers and transaction turn
listeners, not all framework effects. Vue watcher failures differ between
development and production; an enclosing Solid `batch()` can defer errors until
after a handle returns. The guide lists the Link, branch-key, coalesce, pending undo, ordering,
notification, and retention failures documented for 15.3.1, each marked with the
version that repaired it (15.4.0), and Link failures found later that 15.4.4
repairs.


## Collection identity and independent store instances

Declare the store structure and enhancers at construction. `entityMap()` supports
dynamic entity membership; it is not an API for installing new composite slices
with nested marker/enhancer lifecycles. Component/dialog-owned trees are valid:
create one per independent editing session, and call `destroy()` at its owner’s
teardown. A repeated entity ID is not an editing-session ID.

`setAll()` is replacement by key. Repeated incoming keys collapse to the last
value for that key, not distinct rows. Use a required stable ID where available;
validate missing IDs at ingress rather than assigning a shared fallback. Numeric
and string keys remain distinct. Do not depend on a development warning to reject
invalid input. Version 15.3.1 does not warn for non-null duplicate incoming keys.
Since 15.4.4 a batch call naming one id twice applies its copies in order:
`addMany`/`prependMany` strict throws before writing, skip keeps the first copy,
overwrite keeps the last in the first copy's place, and `upsertMany` merges the
copies.

Version 15.4.0 checks `setAll()` staging after user callbacks.
If an interceptor or ID selector changes collection membership, keys or order,
the outer replacement refuses before applying its staged writes. The callback's
already-completed writes remain. Field-only callback writes do not trigger this
structural refusal. Prefer interceptors that validate or transform input instead
of changing the same collection's topology. Since 15.4.4 `addOne`, `addMany`,
`prependOne`, `prependMany`, `upsertMany`, `updateMany` and `removeMany` also
throw `Cannot <method>: collection topology changed during staging` before
writing when a callback changes the collection's membership or order, or the
key of a row the call names; move cascades to a tap or a separate call.

Undo, redo, `jumpTo()` and rollback replay recorded values: since 15.4.4 they do
not run a collection's interceptors, and taps fire for the changes they apply
(`onAdd` for a row they bring back, `onRemove` for one they take away,
`onUpdate` for a changed value). `getCurrentIndex()` follows `undo()` and
`redo()`; steps back are `getCurrentIndex() + 1`. An ordinary write after an
`undoable()` one does not remove its undo: undo restores the turn's own image
over it, and refuses with ST1034 where that would displace a newer row at the
same key. A location under an omitted member reads `undefined`, an entity
collection there reads empty, and writing it re-adds only the written path (see
the kernel README, "Locations an omission has hidden").

In published 15.3.1, calling Link `settled()` immediately after a write can return
before the newly queued send finishes. Version 15.4.0 repairs this same-turn race:
`settled()` waits for the send queued by the preceding write. It is still not proof
of backend durability, and one generic delay is not a universal synchronization
barrier. The repair does not change the published 15.3.1 artifact. Since 15.4.4
`settled()` also waits for sends caused by writes still queued for delivery,
`tree.destroy()` disposes the tree's Links, `link()` on a destroyed tree throws,
and a collection endpoint receives reorders (and a `sortComparer` collection
its `all()` order).

## Choosing ownership for editors and devices

See `docs/guides/owned-sessions.md` and the demo `/owned-sessions`. Keep shared
entities in one owned tree. Give each independent editor a unique session ID and
a local draft (native form state or a separate tree); do not key drafts only by
entity ID. Validate against the current application revision and entity lifetime
before applying. Refuse stale saves while keeping the draft, and never silently
retarget it to a replacement record. These are application policies, not kernel
MVCC or remote concurrency protection. A backend must enforce its own version
check. The demo's Apply locally does not acknowledge a server write.

Each connection owns its subscription and tree. Register cleanup and guard late
callbacks. Destroy that session when closed and all remaining sessions at owner
teardown. Keep resources out of serializable rows. Combine display with computed
reads over a registry, not copied state, root grafting or Link mirroring.

Do not invent dynamic slice APIs, draft/fork primitives, or cross-tree settlement.
Use one framework import root. Angular and Solid write `leaf.set(value)`, Vue
writes `leaf.value = value`, and React/neutral write `leaf(value)`. The demo is
Angular-specific evidence, not a cross-framework lifecycle proof.

## Runtime observation (15.4.0)

Tooling can use `transactionLifecycleReader`, `restorationReader`,
`entityMembershipReader`, and `linkStateReader` from
`@signal-tree/kernel/internals`. Each reader exposes a current `snapshot()` and
`subscribe(listener)` for subsequent events. `stateLocationReader(tree).locate()`
maps an effect's or write's position, entity lifetime and `fieldSegments` to its
current structured location, or `undefined` when no longer reachable. Missing capability is not empty
history. These readers do not install enhancers or retain terminal history.

Use actual tree + collection + entity lifetime identity and typed keys; displayed
paths are labels and must never be split into addressing segments. Confirmation
means local settlement, never server acceptance. Link queued jobs are reconciliation
work, not a FIFO of application values. A tool recording these events owns its
bounded retention and must show interruptions, omissions and unsupported sources.
Unsubscribe on view teardown and destroy bounded-lifetime trees. See
[Runtime observation in 15.4.0](https://github.com/JBorgia/signal-tree/blob/v15.4.0/docs/guides/runtime-observation.md) for contracts and examples.

## Observer failures during undo and rollback (15.4.2)

A reactive observer can throw after undo, redo or transaction rollback has
already applied. SignalTree completes the operation's bookkeeping and rethrows
the original value; a throw alone does not establish that state was unchanged.
Reusing that error in a later failure before application does not make the later
operation successful. Check current state and settlement/history status when
handling failures. This does not provide atomic recovery for arbitrary user
callbacks that partially mutate state before throwing.
